title: A real '3 Body Problem': Astronomers discover a nearby 'weirdo' triple-star system
summary: An international team of astronomers led by the University of Montreal has found a nearby triple-star system, much like the one in the Netflix show 3 Body Problem. But this one seems to be… a little…

image.caption: An artistic illustration shows the Welopō'ai triple-star system, located just 28 light-years from Earth. The system consists of a red dwarf star, right, and a closely orbiting white dwarf, left, with a second white dwarf, upper, orbiting the pair at a much greater distance. (Benoît Gougeon/Universit

blocks.text: Roughly 28 light-years from Earth lies a peculiar star system called IRAS 21500+5903.

For years, astronomers had known about the two stars that orbited one another. But then, when looking for exoplanets — planets that orbit other stars — a group of astronomers made a surprising discovery: there was another star in the system. Instead of being a binary star system, this was a triple-star system.

"It's a freak thing. It was an annoying object," said Étienne Artigau, a researcher at the Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets (IREx) at the University of Montreal. "It's not what we were looking for."
Their findings were released this week in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

The system contains a red dwarf, a type of star that is very common in our galaxy, and two smaller, dense white dwarfs. One is roughly 1,000 astronomical units (the distance between the sun and Earth) away from the red dwarf. The other, they found, was a mere two astronomical units away, a little similar to the distance from the sun to Mars.
The inner white dwarf orbits the red dwarf, while the outer white dwarf orbits the pair.
A quirky neighbour
What's surprising is that no one had discovered it over the decades.

"It's weird that no one found the system, but it also says that there are weird things overlooked just next to us," Artigau said. "It's like not next door, but down the road, just one block away of a stellar neighbourhood."

When a low- to medium-mass star reaches the end of its life, it first swells into a red giant before leaving behind the dense and small white dwarf. It is what will happen to our own sun in roughly five billion years.
This artist concept depicts an ultra-dense dead star, called a white dwarf, passing in front of a small red star. (NASA/JPL-Caltech)

While looking for an exoplanet in this system, the international team of astronomers — led by the University of Montreal team — used an instrument at the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope in Maunakea, Hawaii, called SPectropolarimètre InfraROUge (SPIRou). It is used to detect exoplanets and does this by measuring tiny changes in a star's velocity, which can be caused by orbiting planets.
But the red dwarf wasn't doing what it was supposed to be doing. It was moving differently, with velocity changes of nearly 16 kilometres a second. That's a huge difference.
Initially, they thought it was a brown dwarf, a type of substellar object that has a mass of about 75 times that of Jupiter.
But that still didn't make sense.
More weirdness
The velocities were so off that they broke Artigau's code.

"At some point, we said, Okay, we should get to the end of it. Something's wrong with that object. And so I fixed the code," he said. "And then we just said, let me do the math of that brown dwarf. Okay, no, it doesn't work."
It was a real head-scratcher.

blocks.text: What they eventually discovered is that what was causing the perturbations was a high-mass… something. But it also couldn't be seen.
Could it be a black hole? A neutron star? A white dwarf?

The team turned to the Gemini North telescope, also on Maunakea. Using high-resolution images from its 'Alopeke instrument — a specialized high-speed camera — they found what they were looking for: a faint companion star — a white dwarf — orbiting closely around the red dwarf.
Here's where it gets weirder.

Before becoming a white dwarf, the star would have become a red giant. As it swelled up, its orbit would have been so close to the red dwarf that the pair must have interacted with one another. Many times these types of stars envelop the red dwarf, or the two may even merge. This didn't happen.
And there was more.
The inner white dwarf should be spiralling inward toward the red dwarf. Instead, it is in a stable orbit.
It could be that the more distant white dwarf is somehow stabilizing the orbit, though they don't know yet how. That's for future research.

The image on the left shows the two components of the system: Welopō'ai A, a closely orbiting red dwarf and white dwarf pair, and Welopō'ai B, a second white dwarf located farther away. The image on the right provides a close-up view of the inner pair and their orbital paths. (Pan-STARRS1/STScI/MAST, left, International Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab, right. Graphical construction by Étienne Artigau & Heidi White (UdeM/IREx))
"We're saying it cannot exist," Artigau said. "Of course, it exists. It's there."
Paul Delaney, professor emeritus of physics and astronomy at York University in Toronto, believes that perhaps the more distant white dwarf was once much closer to the other pair.

"I mean, when planetary systems form now, one of the standard things is migration," he said. "I would bet that they were relatively proximate to each other and then they did engage in a bit of gravitational embracing, and the further white dwarf today was much, much closer in its heyday."

To add to the weirdness, the astronomers calculated that the system is roughly 10 billion years old, older than our own solar system of 4.6 billion years, and its stars are metal-rich. Typically, these older stars are metal-poor.
"It's tantalizing, and we just don't know if it means anything. It may just be a random draw basically of a stellar population," Artigau said.
Still searching for an exoplanet

The astronomers gave this system the Hawaiian name Welopō'ai, combining "welo" which means an inherited family trait, and "pō'ai," which means an orbit or circular path. The name therefore means "path of family traits."
The very popular book and Netflix show 3 Body Problem looks at a triple-star system and the effects it could have on a nearby planet, mainly to a civilization that has evolved on that planet.
One of the terms that is used to describe the triple-star system in the show is "chaotic," which affects the speed at which the civilization can evolve.

The issue is an age-old physics problem. Two-body systems are predictable. But add a third, and everything blows up. That's because Body A pulls on Body B and Body C. Body C in turn pulls on Body A and Body B, and because of these interactions, it changes their motions and their forces forever.
While researchers didn't find an exoplanet, Artigau said the search isn't over.
"It's such a weirdo system that Atanas Stefanov, one of the authors, he's applying for time to get, to look for planets around the red dwarf," he said.
Whether there is a planet there or whether an alien civilization could live on a planet in a triple-star system remains to be seen.
For Artigau, he said the fact that something new was thrown at him was very exciting.
"I like it," he said. "Little things that are just sideways in your life in research. It's fun."
